title: Wavefunctions Have a Probabilistic Interpretation
lead: A wavefunction can be complex, so it has no direct physical meaning by itself. Born's interpretation gives its square one, as a probability density, and that reading sets conditions on which functions can be wavefunctions.
objectives: To understand that wavefunctions can have probabilistic interpretations.
To calculate the probabilities directly from a wavefunctions
notes: Adapted from Hanson, Harvey, Sweeney and Zielinski's Quantum States of Atoms and Molecules under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; Example 3.4.1 is set as an exercise, keyed by the solution Section 3.6 prints under Exercise 3.6.1, which asks the same question.

exercises.prompt: Show that the square of the modulus of $\Psi(\vec{r},t) = \psi(\vec{r}) e^{-i\omega t}$ is time independent. What insight regarding stationary states do you gain from this proof?

answer.hint: Write the complex conjugate of the time factor and multiply.
answer.solution:
The square of the modulus of a wavefunction is $\Psi(r,t)^*\Psi(r,t)$ so for wavefunctions of this form, the square of the modulus is

$$ \begin{aligned} \Psi(r,t)^*\Psi(r,t) &= \psi(r) \cancel{e^{+i\omega t}} \psi(r) \cancel{e^{-i\omega t}} \\[4pt] &=\psi(r)^2 \end{aligned} $$

Hence, there is no time dependence to the modulus of wavefunctions of this work, which from the probability interpretation of the wavefunction means that the probability density is time-independent.

exercises.prompt: According to the Born interpretation, what is the physical significance of $e\psi^*(r_0)(r_0)d\tau$?

answer.hint: Start from what $\psi^*\psi\,d\tau$ means, then multiply by a charge.
answer.solution:
By the Born interpretation, $\psi^*(r_0)\psi(r_0)\,d\tau$ is the probability of finding the electron in the volume element $d\tau$ at the point $r_0$. Multiplied by the charge of the electron, $e$, it is the charge expected in that volume element: $e\psi^*\psi$ is a charge density, and $e\psi^*(r_0)\psi(r_0)\,d\tau$ is the share of the electron's charge found in $d\tau$ at $r_0$, averaged over many measurements.

A single measurement still finds the whole electron at one place. The charge density describes where the electron is found over many measurements, in the same way the grade distribution of a class describes many students.

footnotes.html: The book calls $P(x,t)$ the probability amplitude. $P$ is the probability density of Equation 3.4.1; the probability amplitude is the wavefunction itself, as the quoted passage below says.
Equations 3.4.3 and 3.4.4 keep the label $P(x\in[a,b])$ of the one-dimensional case. In three dimensions the integral is the probability that the particle is found in the volume $V$.
The book prints $e\psi^*(r_0)(r_0)d\tau$, with the second $\psi$ missing. The quantity meant is $e\psi^*(r_0)\psi(r_0)d\tau$.
The first line drops the complex conjugate of $\psi(r)$. With it the product is $\psi^*(r)\psi(r) = |\psi(r)|^2$, which is still independent of time.
